extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic and philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic treatment and classification of 'nameable things' (feelings, substances, attributes) and an elementary account of propositions (subject, predicate, copula), including distinctions among qualities, relations, and quantities and the nature of predication. Aimed at clarifying conceptual confusions (e.g., copula and existence, identity vs resemblance) and preparing for analysis of propositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of nameable things
rubrics_metrics.description: All nameable things are classified into four exhaustive classes: (1) Feelings or states of consciousness; (2) Minds which experience those feelings; (3) Bodies (external objects) which excite certain feelings together with the powers/properties by which they excite them; (4) Successions and co-existences, likenesses and unlikenesses between feelings or states of consciousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This fourfold enumeration is offered as a substitute for traditional 'Categories' and is to be used as the basis for analyzing the signification of names and for later inquiry into propositions. Practical application follows when examining what the mind actually assents to in propositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subdivision of feelings
rubrics_metrics.description: Feelings (states of consciousness) are of four sorts: sensations, thoughts, emotions, and volitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perceptions are a case of belief (a kind of thought); actions are volitions followed by an effect. If any other mental state exists, it's unnecessary to discuss it here for the present analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of substances: bodies and minds
rubrics_metrics.description: Substances are either bodies or minds: bodies are the unknown causes of sensations; minds are the unknown percipient experiencing those sensations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: We can know of Matter only insofar as it gives sensations and the order of occurrence of those sensations. The recognition of bodies and minds as 'substances' is retained for common language and practical purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attributes divided into quality, relation, quantity
rubrics_metrics.description: Attributes are of three kinds—Quality, Relation, and Quantity—and these are grounded upon sensations or other states of consciousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attributes of bodies under Quality or Quantity are defined as the powers those bodies have of exciting certain sensations. Most relations likewise are grounded upon some fact or phenomenon construed as a series of sensations or states of consciousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities grounded on sensations
rubrics_metrics.description: Qualities (attributes classed under Quality) are known only by the sensations or states of consciousness they excite and may be defined as the powers of objects to excite those sensations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When predicating a quality of a thing, nothing is asserted beyond the sensations or states of consciousness on which the quality is grounded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relations normally grounded on phenomena (series of sensations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Relations (except certain simple kinds) are grounded upon some fact or phenomenon into which the related objects enter as parts, and that fact/phenomenon is known only by a series of sensations or states of consciousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The relation is the capacity of an object to take part with the correlated object in producing that series of sensations. Thus relational predicates ultimately reduce to patterns among sensations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Likeness and unlikeness as sui generis (primitive relations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Likeness (resemblance) and unlikeness (dissimilarity) are peculiar relations that must stand apart as things sui generis; they are attributes grounded on states of consciousness that are themselves peculiar and (so far) unresolvable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resemblance is a feeling — a state of the observer's consciousness — and whether this is a distinct third state or involved in the sensations is debatable but irrelevant to their primacy. Complex cases of resemblance can be resolved into likenesses among parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Succession and simultaneity as primitive relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Antecedence/consequence (succession) and simultaneousness are the simplest relations and do not require any third thing beyond the two items; our consciousness of succession/simultaneity is not an added third sensation but is involved in having two sensations either successively or simultaneously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These relations do not admit of the same kind of analysis as other relations and are part of the fundamental structure of our faculties; we need not attempt further analysis within logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantity grounded on differences in sensations
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences in quantity (e.g., one gallon vs ten gallons) are grounded in differences in the sensations those quantities excite; the distinction 'in quantity' is just the particular way the sensations differ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Logic will not analyze what the difference in sensations is; it's enough that the cognizable distinction lies in the sensations. Quantity, like quality and relation, is ultimately reducible to patterns in sensations or states of consciousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attributes of minds: internal states and effects on others
rubrics_metrics.description: Attributes ascribed to minds consist either in their own habitual states of feeling (ideas, emotions, volitions) or in the effects they produce in other minds (thoughts, emotions excited in observers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some predicate-words (especially terms of approbation or blame) imply both: (a) the habitual internal state, and (b) that consideration of that state excites approbation/disapprobation in others (e.g., 'generous' conveys both).

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective facts grounded on corresponding subjective facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Every objective fact is grounded upon a corresponding subjective (psychological) fact — a series of sensations or states of consciousness — and apart from that subjective fact the objective fact has no meaning to us.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: What we call an objective fact is a name for the unknown process by which the subjective fact is produced; knowledge of objective facts is therefore mediated by subjective states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguity of the word 'same' (identity vs close resemblance)
rubrics_metrics.description: The word 'same' is ambiguous between primary sense (numerical identity of a single object) and secondary sense (very high degree of similarity); failing to distinguish these senses produces confusion and fallacies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: two feelings cannot literally be the same in the sense of numerical identity; saying two persons have 'the same' disease or 'the same' office typically means very similar kinds rather than literal identity. Failure to notice this ambiguity has led to metaphysical errors (e.g., Platonic 'Ideas').

rubrics_metrics.name: Resemblance between relations (analogy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Relations themselves can resemble one another (analogy) when the fundamenta relationis (the facts/phenomena grounding them) exhibit corresponding resemblances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the father/son relation of Priam/Hector may be called the same relation as Philip/Alexander if a close resemblance exists between the underlying facts; degrees of resemblance vary from near indistinguishableness to slight similarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition requires sign of predication (copula or inflexion)
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposition is a portion of discourse where a predicate is affirmed or denied of a subject; besides subject and predicate, a sign is required to indicate predication (an inflexion or a copula such as 'is'/'is not').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without such a sign we cannot infer that two names placed together form a predication. The copula (or verb inflection) functions to mark that one term is affirmed/denied of the other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copula indicates predication but does not necessarily assert existence
rubrics_metrics.description: The copula's function is primarily to indicate predication; although the copula (e.g., 'is') can carry a meaning of existence in other contexts, its use as copula does not necessarily imply that the subject exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration: 'A centaur is a fiction of the poets' uses 'is' as a copula but does not assert the existence of centaurs. Confusing the copula's grammatical role with an ontological assertion of being has led to much metaphysical speculation and error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affirmative vs negative propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Propositions are first divided into affirmative (predicate affirmed of subject) and negative (predicate denied of subject); the copula in negatives includes the sign of negation ('is not').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some logicians prefer to treat 'is' as the sole copula and attach negation to the predicate ('not-dead' as predicate), but this is largely a verbal reformulation with little practical effect; the textbook follows the standard distinction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex attributes resolvable into simpler likenesses
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex cases of likeness (e.g., likeness of wholes made of parts) can be resolved into a composition of simpler likenesses between corresponding parts (e.g., portrait to original composed of many part-resemblances).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This allows analysis of apparently complex resemblance (e.g., successful mimicry) into likeness in posture succession, voice, words, gestures, etc., each ultimately grounded in resemblance of states of consciousness.
